extracted.intended_audience: architects, art historians, artists, and readers interested in architectural criticism and drawing from life
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for describing, drawing, and judging architectural ornament, styles (Byzantine, Lombard, Arab, Renaissance), and the fidelity of architectural illustration. Emphasizes temperament of schools, materials and technique, geometric construction, and truthfulness of on-site sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orders and their authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of classical orders and spurious variants: e.g., 'You may have heard of another order, the Composite, which is Ionic and Corinthian mixed, and is one of the worst of ten thousand forms referable to the Corinthian as their head: it may be described as a spoiled Corinthian.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claimed 'orders' by their derivation and fidelity to the classical types; criticize invented or 'spoiled' orders (Composite, Tuscan, 'Roman Doric', 'Ordre Francais' where appropriate). Prefer recognition of the two great families (Greek/Doric and Corinthian) as representative types rather than proliferation of meaningless variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical construction and proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectural design may be constructed by clear geometric rules: 'if we take five circles in geometrical proportion, each diameter being two-thirds of the diameter next above it, and arrange the circles so proportioned... we shall find that an increase quite imperceptible in the diameter of the circles in the angles, will enable us to inscribe the whole in a square.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess decorative schemes and façades for underlying geometric logic and proportion; such constructions (e.g., circle proportions inscribed in squares) explain line placement and the center of bands and can validate an author's reconstruction of a design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid needless multiplication of 'orders'
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of inventing an 'order' for every head or horn: 'if, instead of rams' horns, you put ibex horns, or cows' horns, or an ass's head at once, you will have ibex orders, or ass orders, or any number of other orders, one for every head or horn.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor restraint: judge architectural systems harshly when they multiply named 'orders' without meaningful structural or stylistic justification; treat such multiplicity as an architectural anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate schools by temper — energy vs refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential differences among architectural schools are 'more in the degrees of their impetuosity and refinement (these qualities being, in most cases, in inverse ratio, yet much muted by the Arabs) than in the style of the ornaments they employ.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing regional styles (Lombard, Byzantine, Arab), prioritize assessment of their temper, energy, and treatment rather than merely cataloguing ornaments; look for degrees of impetuosity, refinement, and how these relate inversely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of Lombard, Byzantine, and Arab temperaments
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific temperament diagnoses: Byzantine = 'perfect rest... exquisite perception of grace and dignity'; Arab = 'restless fever... same perception of grace, but with a restless fever'; Lombard = 'distinguished ... in his love of jest' and strong energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these temperament profiles as criteria to identify and evaluate buildings and ornament: judge whether a work expresses serenity and severe tradition (Byzantine), feverish invention (Arab), or vigorous jesting energy (Lombard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value truth and veracity in on-site sketches
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the sketches of which those plates in the "Seven Lamps" are fac-similes, were made from the architecture itself, and represent that architecture with its actual shadows at the time of day at which it was drawn, and with every fissure and line of it as they now exist.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize drawings made from direct observation (even if rough) because they capture real shadows, fissures, and existing conditions; accept roughness and occasional unsteadiness as preferable to studio-invented precision that does not exist on the building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth over delicate studio finish in illustration
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It does not in the least follow that because a drawing is delicate, or looks careful, it has been carefully drawn from the thing represented... there is not one line of it that exists on the building.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of 'delicate' plates produced from imagination or studio reconstruction; test illustrative plates against the building itself and prefer faithful, even coarse, facsimiles to elegant but fictional representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liveliness and naturalism of carved figures
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The Lombard animals are all alive, and fiercely alive too, all impatience and spring: the Byzantine birds peck idly at the fruit, and the animals hardly touch it with their noses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate figurative sculpture by degree of animation and naturalistic action: Lombard work is praised when figures exhibit vigorous, animal force; Byzantine work is characterized by restraint and languor—use these as comparative standards of expressive success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material choice and technique as evaluative criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast of technique and material: Pavian work = 'cut in a coarse sandstone, in bold relief'; Lucca = 'wrought entirely in white marble and green serpentine... inlaid with exquisite precision — white on dark ground.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge ornamentation partly by materials and technique (relief carving vs inlay, coarse vs exquisite finish), and by how the material affects the arrangement and the viewer's delight; acknowledge preservation differences due to material and environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of geometry to impose order and calm
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Geometry seems to have acted as a febrifuge, for beautiful geometrical designs are introduced amidst the tumult of the hunt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the successful integration of geometric patterns as a means to control earlier 'morbid restlessness' in ornament; geometry is a positive organizing principle that calms chaotic grotesque compositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and recognizability of motifs
rubrics_metrics.description: Example of vine-leaf motif: 'the actual leaf, which is used in the best Byzantine mouldings at Venice, occurs in parts of these Pavian designs... it is thrown about in endless change; four or five varieties of it might be found on every cluster of capitals.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether carved motifs are clearly rendered and recognizable (e.g., vine with grapes), and note variety and expressive use across capitals; clarity of intent in motif strengthens the design's communicative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for patina and caution against injudicious restoration
rubrics_metrics.description: 'may Heaven only, in its benignity, preserve it from restoration, and the sands of the Serchio give it honorable grave.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value original weathering, patina, and historical integrity; be critical of restoration that risks erasing authentic character—preservation may sometimes mean resisting restoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of proportion and perspective in published plates
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Gaily Knight's plate: 'It may serve to give them an idea of its general disposition, and it looks very careful and accurate; but every bit of the ornament on it is drawn out of the artist's head. There is not one line of it that exists on the building.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using published plates as evidence, verify that proportions and ornaments are faithful to the actual building; careful-looking accuracy in print may conceal invented details—cross-check with on-site sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesque subjects as indicators of regional character
rubrics_metrics.description: List of northern quatrefoil grotesques (elephant and castle; boar hunt; dragon with a human head set wrong way; Noah building the ark; four hares fastened by the ears, etc.) used to 'illustrate the feverish character of the Northern Energy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recurring grotesque subject matter and its sequence as diagnostic evidence of a school's imaginative character and energy; catalogue and interpret subjects to read cultural temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative structural evidence across media (wood to stone)
rubrics_metrics.description: On wooden churches of Norway and transformations: 'The inside view of the church of Borgund shows the timber construction of one shaft run up through a crossing architrave, and continued into the clerestory; while the church of Urnes is in the exact form of a basilica.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cross-media (wood and stone) comparisons as evidence for historical development (e.g., origin of vaulting shafts); structural parallels support theories of architectural evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for judging landscape painters: originality and authentic voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Ruskin's evaluation of Turner: 'I think that J. M. W. Turner is not only the greatest (professed) landscape painter who ever lived... I like his later pictures, up to the year 1845, the best; and believe that those persons who only like his early pictures do not, in fact, like him at all.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing painters, prioritize originality, the artist's distinctive power, and phases of work that best express that individuality; prefer works that reveal the artist's true character over pictures that merely resemble others or flatter contemporary taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward sentimental 'Romanist' pictorial influence
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is of the highest importance, in these days, that Romanism should be deprived of the miserable influence which its pomp and picturesqueness have given it over the weak sentimentalism of the English people... I call it a miserable influence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be critical of art or architecture whose appeal rests on mere pomp or picturesque effect that panders to sentimentalism rather than truth or moral seriousness; prioritize sincerity of feeling and structural honesty over decorative sentimentality.
